text.p: Philippine shares tumbled to new two-year lows on Wednesday, forcing the central bank to step in to calm an edgy local currency market hit by concerns the peso could be hurt by the stock market's slump.
"The Philippines is long overdue for a massive shake-out," Crosby UBP Securities director Roman Azanza said, though he called the latest stocks sell-off overdone.

The Manila composite share index slid 60.27 points or 2.23 percent to 2,648.17 at Wednesday's close on continued foreign selling after recent dismal first quarter profits results from some major firms. The index lost 4.54 percent on Tuesday.

Worries that the stock market downturn would prompt foreign investors, who dominate the market, to take the proceeds of their share sales out of the country forced the central bank to hike interest rates to support the peso.
The bank raised its overnight borrowing rate by 0.75 percentage points to 11 percent, lifting the peso to 26.368 to the dollar from 26.37.
Central bank Treasurer Sergio Edeza told Reuters there had been no capital flight after the share market decline and called the interest rate hike a pre-emptive move to calm the market.

Some analysts and traders were starting to think the bloodbath of the past two days, which dragged the main stock market index to its lowest level since early 1995, might be nearing its end as investors began to scent some bargains.
"Investors are not going to stand in the way of a rushing train. So they are standing on the sidelines and slowly picking some that they feel have been unjustly sold down," one foreign broker said.
But other market players said they would be extremely cautious about stepping back into the fragile market.

The market, now more than 20 percent under its all-time peak three months ago, has been dented by fears of a banking and property slump, poor profits at many leading companies and weak investor sentiment about regional markets overall.

"We have a very emotional market and the decision to buy or sell is driven largely by sentiment. The unexciting first quarter profits just add to the negative sentiment," said Helen Alvarez, research head at All Asia Securities.
Two major companies -- beer and food giant San Miguel Corp and Manila Electric Co -- both disappointed investors with announcements of worse than expected earnings.
Analysts said even Wall Street's dramatic 179-point advance on Tuesday failed to help the local market.
Lawrence de Leon, analyst at Dharmala Securities Phils, said that if anything the U.S. rally had the opposite impact by encouraging funds to head West.
But traders noted Wednesday's fall was not as savage as the more than five percent drop on Tuesday.
"Quietly and steadily some foreign funds are bottom fishing," said Louie Bate, managing director for Equities Brokerage Trading at ING Baring Securities Phils Inc said.
But the central bank's rate hike on Wednesday was the second time in two days that it has stepped in to steady local markets.
On Tuesday, it imposed a 20 percent limit on the amount banks could lend to property firms, a move designed to lower the chances that a property slump would sink the banking sector.
Investors have grown increasingly concerned that the Philippines could be hit by banking and property problems similar to those in Thailand.
